items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.

items.title: Star performers always come back down — not because of psychology
items.claim: A rookie has a breakout season. The next year, his performance drops. Headlines say 'sophomore slump' and 'pressure of expectations'. A statistician would have predicted the drop without ever watching a game.

options.text: Extreme observations have a luck component; the next observation typically regresses toward the underlying mean. The 'rookie season' was partially luck; the next season's mean performance reflects underlying skill, with less luck

items.reveal_title: Galton, sons of tall fathers, and luck
items.reveal:
Francis Galton (1886) measured heights of fathers and sons. He noticed: tall fathers tend to have shorter sons, and short fathers tend to have taller sons. Not because fathers' height 'reverts' to a population mean, but because extreme parental heights are partly random (chance of which alleles were inherited from grandparents).

Galton called this 'regression to mediocrity', later 'regression to the mean'. The term 'regression analysis' for fitting lines to data descends from this observation.

General principle: if a measurement combines skill (or any persistent factor) and chance, extreme measurements come from combinations of GOOD skill AND GOOD luck. Replicate the measurement, and on average the luck component will be average — so the second measurement regresses toward the underlying skill mean.

Applications:
- Sports: 'sophomore slump' is regression, not psychology.
- Medicine: patients with extreme symptoms tend to improve at the next visit (regression to a less-extreme baseline). Many treatments look effective in uncontrolled trials simply because of regression.
- Education: 'praise reduces performance, criticism improves it' (Kahneman's famous Israeli pilot training observation) — actually regression after extreme performances followed by interventions.
- Finance: top-performing fund managers tend to revert toward average; investors who chase last year's winners underperform.

Correct analysis requires CONTROL groups or careful baseline modelling. Without them, regression masquerades as 'real' effects.
items.why: Performance fluctuations get psychological explanations they don't need. The math of extreme values guarantees that record-breakers tend to come back down. Understanding regression to the mean dissolves many spurious 'effects'.

items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.
